如果你想玩两三个小时，还是不错的。但是玩的再久些，就能体会到深度不足。玩了很多局，感觉自己赢的局和输的局打法差不多，但搞不懂为什么有的输，有的就钱多到爆炸。很难说学到了什么技巧，可能就是看运气。 ============================================================ 又打了一会，把机器人城的最高等级打过了 我觉得一是其他城市走小人这个机制不好，如果造多建筑，就会稀释关键建筑的价值。但不多造建筑又吃不到建设度加成。不像房东那样明确告诉你，20个前拿了就赚，20个后尽量少拿。这里我实在没找到合理的界限。 机器人城市几乎不考虑跳过，一直拿，虽然策略上低一些，但体验上好了很多。 二是平衡偏差，没有用的道具和流派还是多，尤其是加了商店价格后，没用的更多了。不乱拿那些奇奇怪怪的道具和流派，主资源流就好打了。

Fun and fresh. From the look I was assuming that it was derivative of Luck be a Landlord, but it is its own thing. You drop buildings on the map and workers run around randomly triggering buildings. Buildings generate money and special effects. Periodically you can add new buildings to the landscape. Every round ends with you paying tax and being able to purchase some special upgrades. This doesn't sound super distinct from LBAL and its many progeny, but it really is - your ability to make neighborhoods and watch your workers wander haphazardly gives new strategic depth, different than the "I hope this symbol lands next to that symbol". Don't get me wrong - I love LBAL and its friends, this simply stands more independently.

城镇建造+肉鸽元素游戏，采用逐步变难的积分目标要求，玩家需要在棋盘地图中有策略性规划布局。需要完成若干积分目标才可成功通关，还是有点上难度的！不同建筑存在不同加成，Build虽多但没有比较明显的趋势，不确定性较大，适合策略游戏高手。

[h2]超级都市 [/h2] 这是一场与时间赛跑的游戏，玩家需要在有限的时间内赚够足够多的税款上交，不然则被命令卷铺盖走人。而游戏中并不是与幸运房东类似的回合制玩法，而是时间的循环，每回合所要上交的金额会越来越多，城市中的各个建筑设施都需要市民完成其中的工作就可以获得该设施对应的金额，每个建筑所需要工作的时间也都是不同的。每种设施都有自己独特的能力，其中有几个比较特殊的设施，它们可以在工作后不仅可以获得金钱还可以获得电力，食物，螺丝等三种资源，这些资源作用非常大，像是通过消耗资源来获得大量的金钱，或者消耗资源来激活各种提供增益效果的设施设备，它们创造出了多种流派玩法。 [h2] 真正的工作包分配[/h2] 游戏中获取随机建筑设施的途径只能通过在游戏进行中会根据时间来给予发放，每个回合发放设施的次数也都不同，每轮所有发放都在时间轴上详细标出。每一次发放都是随机提供三个不同的设施给玩家进行选择，如果都不满意也可以消耗刷新次数来进行重新进行抽取，多个相同的建筑还可以进行升级，能大大提升原本建筑的效果。 既然城市提供了这么多的工作岗位，那也需要城市的居民前来上班。在刚开始的时候玩家经营的城市只有两户居民他们会按照一定的规律将城市中所有的工作轮番完成，之后随着城市的不断发展，四周都会建起居民楼，会有越来越多的居民加入到工作之中。 但需要记住，不是有越多的工作位置就越好，在个人体验之后发现基本上场上所有的工作地点都会有人前往，它并不是根据就近原则，找附近的空闲工作，特别是有一些工作地点的时间耗时很长，加上居民在两处工作点中间的移动的路程也要消耗时间。这些都是玩家需要考虑的地方，合理设置每一个建筑的位置，如果后期想要优化，也可以花钱交换场上两个建筑的位置，这样也是适当平衡了整体的游戏节奏，不会因为无法改变位置感到头疼。 [h2] 商店购物，消费起来[/h2] 商店在玩家经营城市中发挥着重大作用，在这里可以购买到刷新设施的次数和移除场上建筑的锤子，还可以购买到许多强力的道具，在这里也可以被称为是遗物，不同品质的遗物之间所带来的效果也相差甚远，如三星级别的遗物——干冰，它的效果是将所有设施的工作时间减少10%，这种群体的争议，基本上是其他品质遗物不能比拟。 而两星级别的遗物基本上都是针对某些类型设施所提供增益，例如能量饮料则是对游戏设施在完成工作时有概率会获得一个电力资源。商店内还提供设施扭蛋，根据购买扭蛋的类型随机抽取三个同类型的设施。 除了这些以外，还能在这里购买地块，地块将会把自身的效果作用在地块上方建设的建筑，例如机器人地块，它可以使设施没有居民在上面工作也会自动进行工作，纯纯高级劳动力了。 [h2] 总结[/h2] 个人体验了十几局游戏以后，感觉该作是比较出色的，肉鸽的随机要素加上城市建筑的构建，再搭配上地块功能和设施升级等设定，使得整体的玩法变得多样。有创意和策略性，你的每一次决策都尤为关键。 [quote]关注鉴赏组：[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45134494]浮生评测[/url] ←"浮生若梦，一鉴倾心，邀您共赏人间烟火" 加入Steam组：[url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/LLFLLFF]浮生评测[/url]←“一起追寻'浮生若梦'般的游戏体验” 开始“浮生若梦”鉴赏组的奇幻之旅！[/quote]

I am currently addicted to this game! When you begin, the mechanics don't make much sense and everything seems really random - but that's the beauty of the game! The more you play, the more things start to make sense! I love the pacing of the game loop. Make a decision for your tile. Sit back watch the results. Make another decision. As things accumulate, you have to option to readjust your set-up! I highly recommend this title!

Too much reliance on RNG. From turn one I'll try to build into something and proceed to get absolutely nothing that works for it. There's no way to influence the RNG besides rerolls which you can maybe afford 1-2 before losing at best. Rerolls are the same currency as what you use to buy things. There's practically no pivot mechanics besides deleting buildings.

SuperTaxCity, developed by soramame-koubou and published by KIC Games, is one of those deceptively simple strategy games that reveals its true identity only after a few runs. At first glance, it looks like a lighthearted pixel-based city builder—small buildings, cheerful residents, tidy grids—but the heart of the experience lies in its economic tension, randomness, and incremental decision-making. Instead of managing infrastructure or long-term city planning, the game challenges you to build a profitable miniature metropolis under strict time pressure, with unpredictable construction options and an ever-looming tax deadline. Each round becomes its own economic experiment, forcing you to balance short-term survival against long-term income potential. The result is a game that feels familiar in presentation but fresh in execution. The main loop revolves around choosing one of three randomly offered facilities each turn and placing it strategically on your limited plot of land. These facilities—restaurants, houses, entertainment venues, industrial buildings, and many more—generate income when residents wander into them. Residents roam freely and behave semi-randomly, introducing both chaos and excitement into every run. Items you acquire along the way modify the behavior of buildings or citizens, encouraging synergies and engine-building strategies. After the timer expires, tax must be paid based on your earnings, and if you haven’t generated enough income, the run ends prematurely. This structure creates a satisfying push-and-pull rhythm: build quickly, hope the citizens cooperate, and pray the next tax cycle doesn’t destroy everything you’ve constructed. What makes SuperTaxCity compelling is the way it rewards adaptability. Because building choices are randomized, no two cities ever unfold the same way. Sometimes you’re showered with commercial properties and must build a consumption-driven economy; other times housing and support buildings appear, encouraging a resident-based strategy. Certain items reshape your priorities entirely, enabling explosive growth if placed intelligently. The game encourages experimentation—testing whether unconventional building combinations can carry you through multiple tax cycles. Slowly, without the player realizing it, the rhythm becomes hypnotic. Even failed runs feel productive, because each attempt teaches new interactions, synergies, and dangers to avoid. Visually, the game embraces a charming, colorful pixel style that prioritizes legibility and personality. Buildings are immediately recognizable, citizens wobble through streets with distinctive silhouettes, and the UI clearly communicates profits, timers, and tax burdens. The presentation supports the emotional tone of the game—cheerful on the surface, stressful underneath. The soundtrack complements the light city-building fantasy, creating an atmosphere that feels welcoming even as the tax counter ticks down like a bomb. It is clear the developer values clarity over spectacle, and that restraint works in the game’s favor, ensuring the player focuses on decision-making rather than visual clutter. Because SuperTaxCity borrows design sensibilities from roguelike deck-builders, it also inherits some of their frustrations. Randomness can occasionally feel punishing, particularly when you desperately need income-generating buildings but are offered only niche support structures. A run can collapse not because of poor planning but because the draft refused to cooperate. For players who dislike RNG as a central design feature, this unpredictability may feel unfair rather than challenging. The game’s claim to city-building may also mislead players expecting detailed urban simulation—there are no roads to lay, utilities to balance, or zoning decisions to navigate. The focus is almost entirely on economic synergy rather than urban realism, and expectations should be set accordingly. Still, within its chosen design space, SuperTaxCity excels. It is a compact game that respects the player’s time, quickly ramps up strategic thinking, and offers replay value through endless run variations. It occupies a sweet spot between accessibility and depth—easy to learn but genuinely demanding when pursuing high scores or long survival streaks. Its price point and low system requirements make it approachable for a wide audience, especially those who want something strategic but not time-consuming or mechanically overwhelming. And despite its simplicity, it manages to generate stories—runs where a single building or item transformed a doomed city into a thriving one, or where a perfect plan collapsed moments before tax day. SuperTaxCity ultimately shines because it reframes city management as a series of tense, clever micro-decisions rather than slow, sprawling simulation. It captures the addictive spirit of economic roguelikes while maintaining a unique identity, blending charm, strategy, luck, and humor into a compact package. Players looking for a thoughtful, replayable, risk-reward puzzle will find plenty to enjoy here. Those craving realism or narrative depth may move on quickly, but for everyone else, SuperTaxCity is a small but engaging surprise—one worth returning to run after run, just to see what kind of city chance and strategy will build next. Rating: 8/10

"Fun Start, Frustrating Finish." My first impression of Super Tax City was genuinely positive. The opening hour is smooth, cozy, and surprisingly engaging. The pacing feels just right early on: you’re placing buildings, lining up synergies, and watching your tax score climb in a way that feels clever and earned. The game nails that “one more turn” vibe right out of the gate — something that’s harder than it looks for smaller roguelike-style puzzle games. At its core, the game asks you to place buildings based on city-building logic to trigger combos and boost your score. It’s conceptually simple, but when the pieces fall into place, it’s really satisfying. Lining up the right neighborhoods or combining certain building types gives that classic dopamine hit you’d expect from a score-chaser. Like many roguelikes that don’t get their randomness tuned well, Super Tax City eventually hits a wall — and that wall is the RNG. Far too often, you’re left waiting for a specific building type to appear. Runs stall not because you misplayed or took a risk, but because the deck just refuses to give you anything remotely useful for 10, 15, sometimes 20 placements in a row. Instead of feeling strategic or reactive, the game becomes a waiting game — and not a fun one. It’s like planning a combo that you know the game wants you to build… only for it to never show up. The result is this weird mix of boredom and irritation where you’re stuck placing throwaway buildings hoping for a miracle. The aesthetics are honestly lovely. The pixelated visuals have a cute and cozy charm that fits the tone perfectly. It’s the kind of game you want to like because everything is inviting and low-pressure at first. The music adds to the mood too — soft, breezy, and relaxing — though after a while it becomes repetitive enough that you may catch yourself lowering the volume. Super Tax City has a strong concept, a great vibe, and a promising core loop. The first hour showcases what the game could be if the RNG were more balanced or if the player had more tools to mitigate it. But right now, the randomness is tuned too harshly, too stingily, and too often blocks progression in a way that feels unfair rather than challenging. It creates artificial difficulty instead of meaningful choices.

Super Tax City is one of those 'build a scoring engine through synergies' type of games, and those can be very hit and miss for me. This one is a hit. It's quite boardgamey in many ways, with some buildings generating resources that are required by others, buildings that score from spatial positioning in relation to other things, etc. It works very well here, and while it won't scratch the city builder itch if you were after SimCity, the premise does make logical sense in terms of how different buildings key off each other. It's a good one, well worth checking out.
